metadata.title: Qualcomm Stock's Biggest Risk Is The Gap Between Pain And Payoff

content.text:
Just over half of revenue still leans on a shrinking handset market, and the businesses meant to replace it do not reach their targeted scale for years.
How Far Has The Market Already Marked This Stock Down?
At $151, the stock has given back 6.9% across its last two sessions, leaving it at about 58% of its 52-week high of $259.9 and below both its 50-day average of $199.28 and its 200-day average of $167.93. Over the past year, it is down 4.5% while the S&P 500 returned 17.7%. The market is not ignoring the risk. The harder question, if you own it, is whether it is in the price or only starting to arrive.
How Much Of The Company Still Rides On Handsets?
Just over half. Qualcomm (QCOM) reported $9.9 billion of revenue in fiscal Q3 2026, and $5.1 billion came from handset chips inside QCT, a number management ties to industry-wide memory dynamics squeezing the smartphone market. The slowdown behind it is not fresh. Revenue over the trailing twelve months is $44.1 billion, up 1.9% year over year against a 15.8% pace a year earlier, and the quarterly year-over-year rate has run 10.0%, then 5.0%, then -3.5%, and -4.0% in the most recent quarter.
Why Is The Revenue Guide Rising While The Earnings Guide Falls?
Because the cost of building the chips is climbing faster than the selling price. Management's fiscal Q4 2026 guidance puts revenue at $9.7 billion to $10.5 billion, above the $9.6 billion guided for fiscal Q3, and non-GAAP earnings per share at $2.05 to $2.25, a range whose midpoint sits below both the $2.20 guided for that quarter and the $2.21 actually delivered. By its own account, the industry is absorbing a broad-based increase in input costs across wafer fabrication, assembly, test, advanced packaging and memory, and QCT gross margins will sit slightly below their historical range; the baseline business normally runs a 48% to 50% gross margin. Price increases in the double digits are meant to start closing that gap over the next couple of quarters.
What Could Push The Recovery Further Out?
Two things, both from the company's own disclosures. The first is Apple: management now expects the step-down in Apple product revenue to accelerate from fiscal Q4 2026, with its share of the upcoming iPhone launch materially below the 20% previously estimated, and Apple product revenue falling roughly 50% from that September quarter to the December quarter that follows. The second is that the replacement business arrives at a thinner margin: early data center revenue comes from custom chip work, an effect management sizes at a drag of 1.5% to 2% on QCT's weighted average gross margin. Management targets $40 billion of non-handset revenue by fiscal 2029, with data center revenue forecast to build from $5 billion in fiscal 2027 to $15 billion in fiscal 2029. That would reshape a company that turned over $44.1 billion in the past twelve months, and it is years out.
